author: A Robot
objectives: Describe Mars's observed retrograde episode as eastward prograde drift, a stationary point, westward retrograde loop, a second stationary point, and return to eastward motion.
Explain apparent retrograde motion of outer planets in the heliocentric model as Earth overtaking a slower planet on an inner orbit.
Compare the geocentric epicycle explanation with the heliocentric explanation and justify why the heliocentric model is more parsimonious.
Predict the orbital configuration for outer-planet retrograde motion: near opposition, with Earth between the Sun and the outer planet.
Compare the apparent retrograde loops of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn and relate smaller loops to greater distance and reduced parallax.

modules.moduleName: Scene 1 — Mars Reverses Against the Night Sky
modules.description: A guided Earth-based observing scene shows Mars moving across labeled ecliptic constellations over six months, including its westward retrograde loop.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify prograde and retrograde portions of Mars's apparent path.
Describe the role of background constellations as a fixed reference frame for apparent planetary motion.
Recognize stationary points before and after the retrograde interval.
instructions: Face the curved star panel and use Next to step through the six-month sequence.
Watch the red Mars marker relative to Leo, Virgo, Libra, and Scorpius.
Use the growing trail to summarize the complete apparent path.

components.text: Leo        Virgo        Libra        Scorpius
Mars over six months
Start: Mars near Leo

clips.changeMeaning: The night sky, constellation labels, and Mars at its starting point appear to establish the Earth-based observational frame of reference.
clips.narration: We begin from Earth's surface, looking at Mars against the distant stars. The constellations along the ecliptic act like a backdrop for measuring Mars's nightly position.

components.text: Months 1–2: eastward prograde drift

clips.changeMeaning: Mars shifts eastward and a short trail appears, representing the first two months of normal prograde motion.
clips.narration: For about two months, Mars drifts slowly eastward against the stars. This usual eastward apparent motion is called prograde motion.

components.text: First stationary point: apparent motion halts

clips.changeMeaning: Mars is enlarged at the first stationary point before being placed onto the retrograde portion of the loop, emphasizing the reversal.
clips.narration: Then Mars slows and seems to stop. This stationary point marks the beginning of a reversal in its apparent motion.

components.text: Months 3–4: westward retrograde loop

clips.changeMeaning: Mars moves westward and the trail broadens into a loop, showing the roughly fifteen-degree retrograde excursion.
clips.narration: For roughly two months, Mars appears to move westward, tracing a loop about fifteen degrees across. This is apparent retrograde motion—the puzzle that challenged early astronomy.

components.text: Complete apparent path: east → west loop → east

clips.changeMeaning: The completed loop is displayed with Mars moving eastward again, summarizing the full observed sequence.
clips.narration: After a second stationary point, Mars resumes eastward motion. The trail records the full pattern: east, stop, west, stop, and east again.

modules.description: A mechanical geocentric model places Earth at the center while Mars rides on an epicycle whose center moves on a deferent, producing apparent retrograde motion with tuned circular motions.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Define deferent and epicycle in the geocentric model.
Explain how an epicycle can make Mars appear to move backward from Earth.
Evaluate why increasingly complex epicycles reduce explanatory simplicity.
instructions: Observe Earth at the center of the tabletop model.
Watch Mars move from point to point on the epicycle and deferent.
Compare the explanatory power and complexity of the model.

components.text: Geocentric model: Earth fixed at center\nDeferent = large circle; epicycle = small circle

clips.changeMeaning: The Earth-centered deferent and Mars-bearing epicycle are introduced with labels, making the geocentric mechanism explicit.
clips.narration: In the geocentric explanation, Earth stays fixed at the center. Mars rides on a small circle called an epicycle, whose center rides around Earth on a larger circle called the deferent.

components.text: Epicycle + deferent: tuned circular motions

clips.changeMeaning: The epicycle center and Mars are moved along the deferent to demonstrate combined circular motion as an engineered explanation for the loop.
clips.narration: As the deferent carries the epicycle around Earth, Mars also moves on the epicycle. Combined circular motions can be adjusted to mimic the observed loop.

components.text: Inner epicycle segment can produce apparent backward motion

clips.changeMeaning: Mars is placed on the inner side of the epicycle closest to Earth and the sight line swings backward to show the mechanism for apparent retrograde motion.
clips.narration: When Mars is on the inner side of the epicycle—the side nearest Earth—its epicycle motion can briefly dominate and make the line of sight shift backward.

components.text: Works as calculation machinery, but requires many tuned circles

clips.changeMeaning: The label changes to emphasize model complexity, and Mars is moved to a new tuned position to indicate that many parameters must be adjusted.
clips.narration: The model can reproduce retrograde loops, but it needs carefully chosen sizes and speeds. As observations improved, more circles were often added, making the system increasingly complicated.

modules.description: A Sun-centered tabletop solar-system view shows Earth on a faster inner orbit overtaking Mars on a slower outer orbit, naturally producing the retrograde event from Earth's moving viewpoint.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Relate Earth’s shorter orbital period to faster angular motion around the Sun.
Explain why Earth overtakes Mars approximately every 26 months.
State that Mars does not physically loop backward in the heliocentric model.
instructions: View the solar system from above the orbital plane.
Follow Earth on the blue inner orbit and Mars on the red outer orbit.
Notice when Earth passes Mars on the inside track.

components.text: Heliocentric model: Earth and Mars follow smooth orbits
Earth: 1 AU, 1 year     Mars: 1.52 AU, 1.88 years

clips.changeMeaning: The Sun-centered model appears with Earth on the inner orbit and Mars on the outer orbit to introduce the heliocentric frame.
clips.narration: In the heliocentric model, the Sun is central. Earth orbits at one astronomical unit in one year, while Mars orbits farther out at about one point five two astronomical units in one point eight eight years.

components.text: Earth gains on slower Mars

clips.changeMeaning: Earth is advanced farther around its orbit than Mars to visualize its greater angular speed on the smaller orbit.
clips.narration: Earth moves faster around the Sun than Mars. Over the same interval, Earth gains angular distance on the slower outer planet.

components.text: Opposition: Earth overtakes Mars

clips.changeMeaning: Earth and Mars are placed nearly along the same outward direction and an arrow highlights the inside-track overtake geometry near opposition.
clips.narration: Roughly every twenty-six months, Earth catches up and overtakes Mars. Near opposition, Earth lies between the Sun and Mars, passing on the inside track.

components.text: No epicycles: smooth orbits create an apparent sky loop

clips.changeMeaning: Earth is shown after passing Mars while both planets remain on smooth orbit rings, reinforcing that no physical loop occurs in space.
clips.narration: From this outside view, Mars never makes a backward loop. Both planets keep following smooth heliocentric paths; the loop is an apparent pattern caused by the moving viewpoint on Earth.

modules.moduleName: Scene 4 — Connecting Orbit Geometry to the Sky
modules.description: A side-by-side model links the heliocentric orbit view to the Earth-sky view by extending a line of sight from Earth through Mars to a star panel.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Map a line of sight from Earth through Mars to Mars’s apparent position among background stars.
Explain why the projected position reverses during Earth’s overtake.
Distinguish apparent geometric motion from an optical illusion.
instructions: Compare the mini solar-system view on the left with the sky panel on the right.
Follow the yellow line from Earth through Mars to the star panel.
Notice that the sky dot reverses when the line of sight reverses.

components.text: Line of sight projects orbital geometry onto the starfield

clips.changeMeaning: The left heliocentric mini-model, right star panel, Mars dot, and sight line appear together to connect the two perspectives.
clips.narration: The two perspectives now appear together. The left side shows the orbital geometry, while the right side shows where Mars appears against the stars from Earth.

clips.changeMeaning: The line of sight and apparent Mars dot shift eastward before the overtake, showing normal projection across the starfield.
clips.narration: Before Earth overtakes Mars, the Earth-to-Mars line of sight sweeps eastward across the background stars. The apparent Mars dot on the sky panel follows that sweep.

components.text: Retrograde is caused by changing line-of-sight geometry

clips.changeMeaning: The line of sight rotates backward during overtake and the sky-panel Mars dot retraces westward, directly linking the geometry to retrograde motion.
clips.narration: During the overtake, the line of sight reverses. At the same time, the apparent Mars dot retraces westward on the star panel—the retrograde part of the loop.

components.text: One event, two views: smooth orbits produce a sky loop

clips.changeMeaning: After the overtake, the line and apparent dot resume eastward motion and the completed trail reinforces the projection explanation.
clips.narration: After Earth passes Mars, the line of sight resumes its eastward sweep. Retrograde motion is a real apparent motion produced by geometry, not a flaw in perception.

modules.description: Students walk or step through an inner orbit path while viewing a Mars target against distant stars, experiencing the apparent reversal through their own changing viewpoint.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Experience apparent displacement caused by observer motion.
Connect the student's motion on an inner path to Earth's orbital motion.
Explain why the apparent reversal is strongest near closest approach.
instructions: Stand on or near the glowing floor orbit path.
If space allows, walk slowly along the circle while keeping Mars in view; otherwise use Next to simulate positions.
Compare Mars with the background star wall as your observing position changes.

components.text: You are Earth: move your viewpoint and watch Mars shift

clips.changeMeaning: The floor orbit, observer marker, Mars target, and distant star wall appear to stage an embodied model of Earth overtaking an outer planet.
clips.narration: In this scene, you become the moving Earth. The floor circle represents Earth's orbit, Mars is the nearby target, and the distant stars provide the background.

components.text: Before closest approach: apparent drift in one direction

clips.changeMeaning: The observer marker moves around the inner orbit before closest approach, and the sky pointer shifts across the star wall in the prograde direction.
clips.narration: Before closest approach, changing your observing position shifts Mars against the background stars in one direction, like a parallax effect.

components.text: Closest approach: your line of sight reverses

clips.changeMeaning: At the closest approach position, the apparent pointer reverses and the trail bends, letting the student generate the retrograde effect through viewpoint motion.
clips.narration: Near closest approach, your viewpoint changes most rapidly relative to Mars. The apparent position reverses—the same overtaking effect Earth creates with Mars.

components.text: You generated retrograde motion by changing viewpoint

clips.changeMeaning: The observer marker moves beyond closest approach and the pointer resumes its original direction, completing the embodied retrograde trail.
clips.narration: After you pass the target on the inside path, the apparent shift resumes its original direction. Your own motion has produced the retrograde pattern.

modules.moduleName: Scene 6 — Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn Compared
modules.description: A heliocentric comparison model shows Earth and three outer planets, highlighting why Mars has a larger retrograde loop than Jupiter or Saturn.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Compare approximate retrograde loop sizes for Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.
Explain why greater distance reduces apparent angular displacement from Earth's orbital motion.
Apply parallax reasoning to outer-planet retrograde loops.
instructions: Watch each planet highlighted in turn.
Compare the angular loop gauge as it changes size.
Relate the shrinking gauge to the planet's increasing distance from Earth and the Sun.

components.text: Outer planets: farther distance means smaller apparent loop
Compare apparent retrograde loop sizes

clips.changeMeaning: Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, orbit rings, and a loop-size gauge appear to frame a distance-based comparison.
clips.narration: All outer planets can show retrograde motion, but the apparent loop size differs. Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn sit at increasing distances from the Sun.

components.text: Mars loop: about 15°

clips.changeMeaning: Mars is highlighted and the gauge expands to the largest loop size, representing a roughly fifteen-degree apparent loop.
clips.narration: Mars is the nearest of these outer planets during opposition, so Earth's motion makes a large apparent shift. Mars's retrograde loop can span about fifteen degrees.

components.text: Jupiter loop: about 10°

clips.changeMeaning: The highlight moves to Jupiter and the gauge shrinks, demonstrating a smaller loop due to greater distance.
clips.narration: Jupiter lies much farther away, about five point two astronomical units from the Sun. Earth's orbit subtends a smaller angle there, so the loop is smaller—about ten degrees.

components.text: Saturn loop: about 7° because distance reduces parallax

clips.changeMeaning: The highlight moves to Saturn and the gauge shrinks further, showing that the most distant planet in this comparison has the smallest apparent loop.
clips.narration: Saturn is farther still, near nine point five astronomical units. From that distance, Earth's motion causes an even smaller apparent shift—often around seven degrees.

modules.moduleName: Scene 7 — Prediction Challenge: Place Mars Near Opposition
modules.description: Students use a guided challenge layout to identify where Mars must be relative to Earth and the Sun for retrograde motion to occur, then repeat with Earth in a new orbital position.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Predict that retrograde motion occurs near opposition for outer planets.
Use relative Sun-Earth-Mars geometry rather than absolute position to locate the retrograde configuration.
Interpret an inset sky preview as feedback for a correct Mars placement.
instructions: Use the Mars marker and highlighted orbit arc to reason about the correct configuration.
Look for Earth between the Sun and Mars, with Earth ready to pass on the inside track.
Use the inset sky panel: a loop appears when the configuration is correct.

components.text: Prediction challenge: where should Mars be for retrograde?
Question: where does retrograde occur?

clips.changeMeaning: The challenge model appears with Earth fixed, Mars on its orbit, and an inactive sky inset for testing the prediction.
clips.narration: Now predict the geometry. Earth is fixed on the blue orbit. Mars must be placed where an Earth observer would see a retrograde loop.

components.text: Hint: Sun–Earth–Mars nearly aligned

clips.changeMeaning: A highlighted arc appears near the opposition region, guiding students toward the relative Sun-Earth-Mars alignment.
clips.narration: The key is opposition: Earth lies between the Sun and Mars and is about to overtake Mars from the inside. The highlighted arc marks the likely region.

components.text: Correct: near opposition, Earth overtakes Mars

clips.changeMeaning: Mars is moved to the opposition alignment, and the inset retrograde loop appears as confirmation of the correct prediction.
clips.narration: This placement is correct. Mars is near opposition, Earth is positioned to pass it on the inside, and the inset shows the retrograde loop.

components.text: Same rule after rotation: Mars near opposition

clips.changeMeaning: Earth is moved to a different orbital location and the correct Mars region rotates with it, emphasizing relative geometry rather than absolute position.
clips.narration: When Earth moves to a different place in its orbit, the correct Mars position rotates too. Retrograde depends on relative geometry, not on a fixed location in space.

modules.moduleName: Scene 8 — Recap: Puzzle, Models, Geometry, Prediction
modules.description: A closing summary board highlights the observed retrograde phenomenon, geocentric epicycles, heliocentric overtaking, line-of-sight geometry, outer-planet comparison, and prediction rule.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Summarize the full explanatory chain from observation to prediction.
Contrast geocentric complexity with heliocentric parsimony.
Recall the final rule for predicting outer-planet retrograde motion.
instructions: Read the highlighted summary item as the narrator reviews it.
Use Previous to revisit earlier concepts if needed.
Complete the lab when you can state the final prediction rule in your own words.

components.text:
1. Observed Mars loop
2. Geocentric epicycles
3. Heliocentric overtaking
4. Line-of-sight geometry
5. Mars > Jupiter > Saturn loop size
6. Prediction: retrograde near opposition

2. Geocentric epicycles

clips.changeMeaning: The highlight moves to the observation item and the Mars icon is enlarged to recall the original sky-path puzzle.
clips.narration: First, you observed Mars's apparent path: eastward drift, a stationary point, a westward loop, another stationary point, and resumed eastward motion.

components.text:
1. Observed Mars loop
2. Geocentric epicycles  ← works, but grows complex
3. Heliocentric overtaking  ← simpler relative motion
4. Line-of-sight geometry
5. Mars > Jupiter > Saturn loop size
6. Prediction: retrograde near opposition

clips.changeMeaning: The highlight covers the geocentric and heliocentric explanation items, and both model icons enlarge to contrast the explanations.
clips.narration: Second, you compared models. Geocentric epicycles can reproduce the loop, but with tuned machinery. Heliocentrism explains the event more simply as Earth overtaking Mars.

components.text:
1. Observed Mars loop
2. Geocentric epicycles
3. Heliocentric overtaking
4. Line-of-sight geometry  ← viewpoint creates apparent reversal
5. Mars > Jupiter > Saturn loop size  ← distance effect
6. Prediction: retrograde near opposition

clips.changeMeaning: The highlight shifts to line-of-sight geometry and planet comparison, summarizing why the apparent reversal happens and why more distant planets have smaller loops.
clips.narration: Third, you linked orbit geometry to the sky using a line of sight. You also saw that Mars has the largest loop, while Jupiter and Saturn have smaller loops because they are farther away.

components.text:
Final takeaway:
Retrograde motion occurs near opposition,
when faster Earth overtakes a slower outer planet.
Smooth heliocentric orbits naturally explain the apparent sky loop.

clips.changeMeaning: The highlight expands and the final rule replaces the list, ending the lab with a concise prediction statement.
clips.narration: Final rule: an outer planet shows retrograde motion near opposition, when faster Earth overtakes the slower outer planet. The planet does not physically reverse; our moving viewpoint makes its sky position reverse.
